Bring architectural discipline, The Standard and familiar software-engineering principles into the normal .NET build. One package reference turns structural expectations into guidance developers can see and act on while they write code.

Architecture that participates in the build

Architecture is easiest to maintain when it is part of everyday development rather than a diagram that is reviewed after the code has already drifted. cCoder.CodeAnalysis analyses the Roslyn compilation, identifies the role played by each type and reports violations through ordinary compiler diagnostics. The same feedback appears in the Visual Studio Error List, editor integrations and command-line or continuous-integration builds.

Each diagnostic has a stable code and a dedicated documentation page. The message identifies the rule that was broken; the documentation explains the relevant part of The Standard, why the constraint matters and shows bad and good implementations. This turns an architectural warning into practical guidance rather than leaving developers to reverse-engineer an undocumented convention.

Established principles, made mechanically visible

The library is built around The Standard, but the values it protects are not isolated to one methodology. They reinforce widely respected industry practices such as SOLID, separation of concerns, dependency inversion, explicit contracts, cohesive components and predictable failure boundaries.

  • Single responsibility and separation of concerns: models carry data, services provide functionality, brokers isolate external resources and exposures translate transport concerns. Validation, exception handling and application composition each have an explicit home.
  • Dependency inversion: services consume local interfaces and dependencies flow through deliberate architectural layers. External packages are contained behind brokers instead of leaking their types and behaviour throughout the application.
  • Interface segregation and cohesive contracts: service APIs stay focused on one business model and expose only the operations promised by their local interfaces.
  • Open, maintainable composition: processing, orchestration, coordination, management and aggregation services combine smaller capabilities without turning one class into an unrestricted dependency hub.
  • Readable, predictable code: naming, asynchronous returns, source layout, formatting, validation collectors, exception mappings and test structure follow consistent conventions across the project.

Static analysis cannot prove that a design is perfect, but it can make structural drift, accidental coupling and inconsistent implementation choices immediately visible. That shortens review cycles and gives both developers and AI coding agents a shared, executable definition of the codebase they are expected to extend.

Highly structured without becoming inflexible

The analyser does more than check class names. Its diagnostic families describe how architectural elements may depend on one another, where business operations belong, how public contracts are shaped, where validation and exception protection occur, and which layer should own looping, branching or coordination. A codebase that follows those boundaries is easier to navigate because similar problems are solved in similar places.

That consistency pays off as the system grows. A new contributor can infer the purpose of a type from its name and location; a reviewer can spot an invalid dependency without reconstructing the whole application; and a change is less likely to spread through unrelated layers. The result is not structure for its own sake, but a maintainable system whose responsibilities and flow remain legible over time.

Enable it with one package reference

Add cCoder.CodeAnalysis to every project that should be analysed:

<PackageReference Include="cCoder.CodeAnalysis" Version="2026.7.22.0000" />

No separate analyser or build-task package is required. Restore and build the project as normal; the package contributes its analyser to the compilation and reports STX diagnostics through the existing .NET toolchain. The current build integration requires the .NET 10 SDK.

What happens when the project builds

  1. The analyser inspects the C# compilation and classifies recognised Standard element types.
  2. Applicable architectural, contract, validation, exception, naming, testing and formatting rules are evaluated.
  3. Findings are emitted as compiler diagnostics with links to the corresponding guidance in this documentation.
  4. For a successful non-test build, the package generates project.stxjson beside the project file and avoids rewriting it when the architecture has not changed.

The portable architecture document records types, members, fully qualified type names, directed internal relationships and analysis items. It can be consumed by Visual Studio or browser-based tooling to visualise the same architecture that the compiler has evaluated. Test projects are still analysed, but do not generate the document.

Adopt the rules as a development feedback loop

Start by adding the package and building the existing solution. Treat the initial diagnostics as a map of architectural decisions that are currently implicit or inconsistent, then resolve them one family at a time. Because the rules run in local builds and CI, improvements remain enforced after the first cleanup instead of depending on reviewers remembering every convention.

The diagnostic groups below are the complete reference. Open a group to understand its architectural scope, then follow an individual diagnostic to its Standard evidence, rationale and code examples.
